name: Event-Driven Trading
title: Event-Driven Trading
answer: Event-driven trading is the practice of taking positions around discrete corporate or regulatory events, such as earnings releases, merger announcements, index changes, and court rulings. In the AI sector, those events include model releases, chip supply news, data licensing deals, and the 148 active AI lawsuits the site tracks. The scope also covers the instruments affected, from the 117 listed AI-related instruments to private companies that may be acquired. The aim is to price the event's probability and impact rather than to forecast long-term trends.

sections.body: Event-driven trading is the practice of taking positions around discrete corporate or regulatory events, such as earnings releases, merger announcements, index changes, and court rulings. In the AI sector, those events include model releases, chip supply news, data licensing deals, and the 148 active AI lawsuits the site tracks. The scope also covers the instruments affected, from the 117 listed AI-related instruments to private companies that may be acquired. The aim is to price the event's probability and impact rather than to forecast long-term trends.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Event-driven trading systems run on market data feeds, news wires, regulatory filing systems, and alternative data sources. For AI events, that can include SEC filings, court dockets, patent databases, and the 355 merger and acquisition filings the site tracks. The infrastructure often combines a low-latency data pipeline with a research environment for backtesting and a risk system that can halt trading when data quality drops. Cloud compute and message queues are common, as are vendor APIs for news and filings.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with defining an event taxonomy, then building a pipeline that detects, classifies, and timestamps each event. Natural language processing models can extract entities, sentiment, and surprise from filings, press releases, and transcripts, while statistical models estimate the expected move and the probability of completion for deals. Traders and analysts then review the signals, size positions, and manage the spread between the event date and the resolution date. Backtesting must account for look-ahead bias, survivorship bias, and the fact that many events are announced after market close.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Event-driven trading raises questions about data rights, because news feeds, court records, and alternative data all carry license terms. Provenance matters: a signal is only as good as its source, and the site's 219 compliance and regulation pages show how much rule-making surrounds AI. Risk includes market risk, model risk, and operational risk, such as a misclassified event or a delayed feed. Firms also need to handle material non-public information carefully, with information barriers and audit trails.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward faster event detection, with large language models reading filings and transcripts in near real time. More events are becoming machine-readable, from structured regulatory feeds to standardized court data, which reduces manual tagging. At the same time, the number of AI-related events keeps growing, as the 148 active AI lawsuits and 355 merger filings suggest. Expect more integration between event-driven signals and portfolio construction, with human oversight focused on edge cases and data provenance.
